slide_002.text: Let us begin by understanding what we mean by an inspector. An inspector is anyone who has the responsibility to carry out inspection activities according to the project specification. As described in ISO 12944-8, an inspector can be someone responsible for ensuring conformity with one or more individual specification requirements. So, being an inspector is not simply about checking the work visually. The inspector has a responsibility to verify that the work complies with the requirements defined for the project. The exact responsibilities can vary depending on the project, the specification, and the contractual arrangement. Therefore, before starting inspection activities, an inspector should clearly understand what they are responsible for checking and reporting. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. These may include the specification, procedures, Inspection and Test Plan or ITP, applicable standards, Product Data Sheets or PDS, and Material Safety Data Sheets or MSDS. The inspector should work in the interest of the company while remaining ethical, honest, and loyal. Good reporting is also an important part of the job, so the inspector should know how to prepare inspection reports correctly. In addition, the inspector must know how to use coating inspection instruments properly. Finally, confidential company information must be protected. These responsibilities together form the foundation of professional inspection work. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_005.text: Let us now understand the role of the inspector in Quality Control and Quality Assurance. For a QC Inspector, we can remember the term OADR: Observation, Assessment, Document, and Report. First, the inspector observes and monitors the contractor's activities. Next comes assessment, where the inspector carries out inspection and testing on the completed activities. After that, the inspector documents the observations and assessment results in an inspection report. Finally, the report is signed by the QA Inspector or client inspector, and copies are distributed to the relevant parties. The QA Inspector has a different function. QA checks the documents prepared by QC and may cross-check testing when necessary. In this way, QA works more like an audit function, verifying that the QC process and records are appropriate. The inspector must follow and enforce the specification that applies to the current project. Normally, the inspector's authority and responsibilities are stated in the project specification. If they are not clearly mentioned, these matters should be discussed during the pre-job or kick-off conference. The inspector needs clearly defined authority and responsibilities in order to perform the job effectively. Without clearly established authority and responsibilities, the inspector's role can become unclear and ineffective. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. When authority, responsibilities, inspection methods, and reporting requirements are clearly agreed at the beginning, the inspector can perform the role with greater confidence and consistency. slide_009.text: Technical knowledge alone does not make someone a good inspector. The inspector's attitude and behaviour are also very important. A professional inspector should be properly trained, certified, and have proven knowledge. The inspector should be honest and sincere wherever they are assigned. Good communication is essential because the inspector works with different people and project parties. The inspector should be proactive and capable of making appropriate decisions within their authority. They should always remain quality conscious and maintain a positive attitude. At the same time, they should be polite, calm, and respectful toward everyone. Being a good team player is also important. Finally, inspectors may work with people from different nationalities and backgrounds, so cultural differences must always be respected. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_010.text: So, what makes someone a first-class professional inspector? First, the inspector should be an asset to the company. This means their knowledge, attitude, and performance should contribute positively to the project and the organisation. A first-class inspector should be proactive rather than simply waiting for problems to appear. Communication is another important quality because the inspector needs to work effectively with the client, contractor, supplier, and other parties. The inspector should also maintain an optimistic and constructive approach instead of being pessimistic. Most importantly, honesty and integrity must be demonstrated throughout every stage of inspection. A professional inspector is therefore someone who combines technical knowledge, responsibility, communication, positive behaviour, and strong professional integrity. One approach is to review the available standards and compare them with the project procedure or requirements in order to reach an understanding. If the parties are still not convinced, a third party expert or specialist may be invited. The Third Party Inspector can then analyse the available information, investigate the issue, identify the root cause where required, and provide a technical conclusion or recommendation. The important principle is impartiality. slide_055.text: Corrective action is different from simply fixing a problem. Corrective action involves identifying the root cause of a coating defect or deviation from the specification and implementing measures to prevent the same problem from happening again. A correction fixes the existing non-conformance. Corrective action goes one step further by addressing the root cause. The key elements include identifying the root cause, implementing measures to eliminate that cause, and preventing recurrence.
